name: Vesilute

People interested in longevity use it as part of a wellness routine aimed at the bladder and urinary tract, with some mentions of prostate comfort.

paras: Proponents say the dipeptide supports bladder tissue, smooth muscle and regeneration. The mechanism has not been described in published human studies.

lead: Vesilute is a synthetic dipeptide made of glutamic acid and aspartic acid (Glu-Asp, often abbreviated "ED"), described as a Khavinson-style peptide bioregulator developed at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology.[1] Peptide-database and vendor pages describe it as aimed at bladder, urinary tract and pelvic tissue, and distinguish it from Vesugen, a related tripeptide that targets vascular endothelium.[1]

People in longevity and peptide circles use it as part of a general-wellness routine aimed at urinary and pelvic health, with the reasoning that comfort and vitality help people stay active and keep their physique and energy. Some pages also mention prostate support for men.[1] Its connection to appearance is indirect and claimed rather than direct.

The published research base is small. The database page that lists it cites three general reviews without methods or outcome data and itself states that clinical evidence is limited and that gender-specific research is limited, with the compound mainly studied in men.[1]
infobox: St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology [1]

paras: Vesilute is a two-amino-acid peptide built from glutamic acid and aspartic acid [1]. It belongs to the family of short peptide bioregulators associated with Vladimir Khavinson's group, each of which is marketed as supporting a particular organ or tissue [1].

Vendor and database pages describe it as supporting bladder and urinary tract function, smooth muscle regulation, pelvic blood flow and tissue regeneration; some list prostate comfort for men and relief of benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms as emerging areas.[1] The page rates bladder and urogenital-aging claims as moderate and others as emerging, and says benefits develop gradually over weeks.[1]

The database page presents these as proposals rather than established findings: regulating contraction and relaxation of bladder-wall smooth muscle, improving microcirculation in pelvic tissue, supporting tissue repair and reducing inflammation-related dysfunction, and modulating gene expression through bioregulation pathways.[1] It lists the half-life as not established.[1]

The database page describes the compound as well tolerated in research, with mild injection-site reactions possible, and lists contraindications including hypersensitivity, active urinary tract infection, pregnancy or breastfeeding and prostate cancer.[1] It advises consulting a physician and warns about products of unknown source or unverified purity.[1] It does not state any regulatory approval status.[1]
No studies found. The database page that lists Vesilute cites general reviews of the Khavinson peptide family rather than trials of this dipeptide, and describes clinical evidence as limited [1].
Vesilute is sold mainly by research-peptide vendors and discussed on peptide blogs and database sites. Regulatory status is not addressed on the pages reviewed [1].
